What to expect during monday.com's Elevate event: Join theCUBE Oct. 29
by Cheryl Knight
Enterprise work management is entering a new phase as artificial intelligence agents move beyond assisting employees to executing business processes.
Platforms once designed to organize projects and track assignments are becoming environments where people and autonomous agents collaborate, raising questions about application development, productivity and governance. That transition is a central theme of monday.com's Elevate conference, taking place Oct. 28-29 at the Javits Center in New York City. The event brings together business leaders, developers and technology professionals to examine how AI is changing enterprise operations. SiliconANGLE and theCUBE will provide exclusive interviews and analysis , with special coverage airing Oct. 29. (* Disclosure below.)
"Monday.com Elevate signals a broader shift in application development: from building software that helps people manage work to building AI-powered applications and agents that execute work," said Paul Nashawaty , principal analyst at theCUBE Research. "For AppDev leaders, the promise of AI-assisted app creation is compelling, particularly as business teams seek to build tailored solutions faster and reduce their dependence on constrained engineering resources."
The opportunity is substantial, but so are the challenges of deploying autonomous systems within established enterprise environments. As monday.com expands its AI capabilities, theCUBE will examine whether organizations can translate faster application development into measurable business outcomes while maintaining oversight of increasingly independent agents.
AI-powered application development moves beyond traditional work management
The growing use of AI agents is changing expectations for enterprise work management software. Rather than simply coordinating assignments, these platforms are beginning to execute the work itself, automating processes and giving employees new ways to create applications without extensive coding expertise.
The shift is already evident in enterprise software development, where AI adoption has accelerated significantly.
"The momentum behind events like Elevate is unmistakable. According to theCUBE Research, 92% of organizations now report AI capabilities integrated into at least one stage of their software delivery lifecycle, up sharply from 71% in early 2024," said Sam Weston , analyst at theCUBE Research.
The company's monday AI ecosystem brings together several capabilities intended to support that shift. Agent Factory allows organizations to create specialized AI agents, while monday sidekick provides contextual assistance within the workspace. Meanwhile, monday vibe enables users to build custom business applications through natural-language prompts, reducing the technical expertise traditionally required for software development.
These capabilities could help businesses address application backlogs and automate processes that span departments. Sales teams, for example, could use agents to qualify leads and update records, while service organizations could automate ticket routing and resolution. The broader opportunity is to connect these activities within a shared operational environment.
The Elevate 2026 agenda includes hands-on sessions focused on building AI agents, creating applications with vibe coding and integrating automation into enterprise workflows. The emphasis on practical implementation reflects a growing industry challenge: moving beyond experimental AI applications to systems that deliver consistent results.
The anticipated expansion of autonomous agents adds urgency to these efforts, particularly as enterprises consider how human employees and AI systems will share responsibility for business processes.
"With 79% of organizations anticipating widespread AI agent adoption within three years, Elevate26's focus on building with AI agents and human-agent collaboration arrives at a pivotal moment for enterprise leaders," Weston said.
The real test, however, is whether organizations can move beyond rapid prototyping to production-grade applications with measurable business value, maintainability and enterprise controls, according to Nashawaty.
"Elevate's significance will ultimately be determined not by how quickly an app can be generated, but by how reliably it can be deployed, governed and scaled," he said.
AI agent governance becomes essential as autonomous workflows expand
Giving AI agents greater responsibility across business applications also introduces new security and governance challenges. Agents that can access sensitive information, modify records or initiate transactions require clearly defined permissions and oversight mechanisms, particularly when their activities cross organizational boundaries.
For enterprises adopting AI-powered work management, the challenge extends beyond protecting individual applications. Organizations must establish how agents authenticate, what information they can access and which activities require human approval.
"The security question gets more difficult as AI agents move deeper into enterprise workflows. An agent may be acting on behalf of a person, but its access can span applications, data and business processes. Enterprises need a clear way to establish whose authority the agent is operating under, what it is allowed to do, and when a human needs to get involved," said Krista Case , principal analyst and practice lead of cybersecurity and cyber resilience at theCUBE Research.
These considerations become particularly important as business users gain the ability to create applications and automated workflows independently. Faster development can reduce pressure on IT teams, but it can also introduce inconsistencies in security policies, access controls and operational accountability if organizations lack centralized governance.
The Elevate agenda addresses these concerns through sessions dedicated to AI governance and guardrails, offering a broader discussion about what enterprises need to consider before expanding agent deployments.
"Platforms such as monday.com are becoming places where people and AI agents coordinate work together," Case added. "That puts governance directly in the flow of work. Companies need visibility into what agents are doing, controls around the data and actions available to them, and an audit trail that lets teams understand how work moved from a request to an outcome."
For monday.com and its enterprise customers, the next stage of AI adoption will depend on balancing easier application creation with the security and governance requirements of production environments. TheCUBE's coverage will examine how that balance shapes the company's platform strategy and what it means for organizations preparing to give AI agents a more active role in everyday business operations.
TheCUBE event livestream
Don't miss theCUBE's coverage of monday.com's Elevate event on Oct. 29. Plus, you can access theCUBE's exclusive content on demand after the event.
How to watch theCUBE interviews
We offer you various ways to watch theCUBE's coverage of monday.com's Elevate event , including theCUBE's dedicated website and YouTube channel . You can also get all the coverage from this year's events on SiliconANGLE .
TheCUBE podcasts
SiliconANGLE's "theCUBE Pod" is available on Apple Podcasts , Spotify and YouTube , which you can enjoy while on the go. During each podcast, SiliconANGLE's John Furrier and Dave Vellante discuss the biggest trends in enterprise tech, including AI, cloud, cybersecurity and infrastructure, with context and analysis.
SiliconANGLE also produces our weekly "Breaking Analysis" program, where Vellante examines major developments in enterprise tech, combining insights from theCUBE with spending data from Enterprise Technology Research, available on Apple Podcasts , Spotify and YouTube .
Guests
During monday.com's Elevate 2026 , theCUBE will feature interviews focused on the company's AI strategy, Agent Factory, monday sidekick and vibe coding. Discussions will address how AI agents are changing enterprise workflows, the business implications of AI-powered application development and the security and governance challenges of deploying autonomous systems at scale.

Cloud Governance 101: Public Procurement Of Cloud Services
Spice Route Legal
Explore more from Spice Route Legal
The cloud service industry in India has generally been an unregulated space, despite multiple attempts by the government over the past decade to introduce legal and policy frameworks
India Government, Public Sector
Mathew Chacko
Aadya Misra
Author LinkedIn connections
INTRODUCTION
The cloud service industry in India has generally been an unregulated space, despite multiple attempts by the government over the past decade to introduce legal and policy frameworks. The National Telecom Policy, issued by the Department of Telecommunications in 2012, was one of the first policy attempts that addressed the need to adopt cloud computing. In 2018, the Digital Communications Policy replaced the 2012 policy with an aim to establish India as a global hub for cloud computing and create a light touch regulatory framework for the industry. Simultaneously, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India - the nodal telecom regulator - released two consultation papers between 2017 and 2019, with recommendations on cloud services, a proposal for a regulatory framework, and suggestions on the establishment of an industry body to govern and regulate cloud service providers in India. The recommendations were met with significant opposition from leading market players and were put on hold.
Today, there is no single regulation or legal framework that governs cloud services. Nevertheless, cloud services designed for government agencies are not a free-for-all, and certain government initiatives impose obligations on providers that offer cloud solutions to such agencies. This note provides an overview of the regulatory requirements for organisations that seek to provide cloud services to public sector players in India.
THE MEGHRAJ CLOUD INITIATIVE
In 2014, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (" MeitY ") introduced a national government cloud initiative called "MeghRaj". MeghRaj was intended to utilise and harness the benefits of cloud computing and ensure the proliferation of cloud services among government departments and public sector undertakings in a manner that enhanced their e-governance frameworks.
As part of this initiative and specifically to facilitate government procurement and adoption of cloud computing services, MeitY introduced a series of guidelines (" MeitY Guidelines ") to highlight key considerations - particularly, data protection and security compliance requirements - for public procurement of cloud services.
APPLICABILITY OF THE MEITY GUIDELINES
The MeitY Guidelines apply to cloud service providers (" CSPs "), managed service providers, and system integrators that provide cloud services to government organisations, departments, agencies, ministries, autonomous institutions, statutory bodies, offices under the Government of India, states, and union territories, local governments, public sector undertakings, and nationalised banks within India (collectively, " Government Departments ").
Government Departments are permitted to procure cloud services directly (a) from CSPs that are "empaneled" with MeitY, (b) through managed service providers (" MSPs "), or (c) through systems integrators (" SIs "). The General Financial Rules, 2017 clarify that Government Departments may only procure cloud services from empaneled CSPs registered on the Government e-Marketplace platform. In contrast, MSPs and SIs control and manage cloud services provided by empaneled CSPs but are not required to be empaneled themselves. The burden of ensuring compliance with empanelment requirements, registration requirements, and the MeitY Guidelines falls on the service provider. Any violation of these requirements may result in the temporary or permanent suspension of the service provider or de-empanelment of the CSP, in addition to other legal and contractual remedies available to the Government Department.
CSPs can apply to be empaneled for different service models (i.e., IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS) and deployment models (these include public clouds, virtual private clouds, and government community cloud models). Different deployment models are required to comply with different technical requirements. As a baseline requirement, CSPs are required to mandatorily offer a set of "basic cloud services" (for example, virtual machines, database services, storage services, network and security services, etc.) to be empaneled. However, the provision of "advanced cloud services" (for example, data warehousing services, analytics services, and managed services like disaster recovery) is optional, and may be offered by CSPs at additional costs.
Since 2016, MeitY has conducted four rounds of empanelment of CSPs, the most recent of which, ended on August 31, 2021. An approved empanelment application remains valid for three years.
The MeitY Guidelines do not regulate private sector procurement of cloud services.
EMPANELMENT PROCESS
MeitY's empanelment process involves a detailed audit and assessment of the applicant. Once empaneled, MeitY conducts a surveillance audit of the CSP annually.
The empanelment process consists broadly of the following steps:
An applicant submits an application form and details of the proposed cloud services in accordance with the format prescribed in the application document.
MeitY conducts an initial assessment and compliance check to confirm the submission of all requisite
Upon a successful completion of the initial assessment, the applicant is required to have its cloud service offerings and data centres audited by the Standardisation Testing and Quality Certification (" STQC ") which is a MeitY office that determines compliance with MeitY-prescribed data protection and security requirements and standards.
If the applicant successfully passes the STQC audit, MeitY issues a letter of award that certifies the empanelment and publishes details of the applicant on its A list of current providers empaneled with MeitY is available here.
THE GEM PLATFORM
In 2016, the Indian government established a Government to Business (" G2B ") online platform called the Government e-Marketplace (" GeM ") that aimed to make public procurement a transparent process. GeM functions as an online portal for the procurement of goods and services, where sellers can register and bid for government contracts and provide such goods and services. Empaneled CSPs, MSPs, and SIs are mandatorily required to register themselves on the GeM platform and comply with the standard GeM terms and conditions to offer cloud services to Government Departments. These departments may, in turn, procure such services either through the GeM marketplace or through bid and reverse auction facilities available on the GeM platform.
Foreign entities are not permitted to directly sell their products or services on the GeM platform but must appoint and authorise distributors to sell and provide services on their behalf. Once authorised, distributors are required to comply with a detailed vendor assessment, and upon successful completion, may sell their products or services on the platform.
DATA PROTECTION, SECURITY, AND LOCALISATION REQUIREMENTS
In addition to general compliance with the legal requirements imposed under the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the rules, regulations, and directions issued under it, CSPs that seek to be empaneled under the MeghRaj initiative must fulfil detailed data protection, security, and other legal requirements prescribed by MeitY.
This includes compliance with security standards that include ISO 27001:2017 and 20000-1:2018 (for data center facilities), Cloud Security ISO Standard ISO 27017:2015, and Privacy Standard ISO 27018:2019. Additionally, CSPs must provide an intrusion detection system, deploy anti-malware tools, and implement service and operational management processes and procedures, incident management procedures, backup services, cloud storage requirements, and disaster recovery and business continuity plans. MeitY requires CSPs to contractually impose these obligations on their subcontractors and sub-processors as well.
Perhaps the most crucial aspect of the MeitY Guidelines is the data localisation requirement, which is in line with the Indian government's overarching stance on data sovereignty and heightened security requirements for data held by Government Departments. All data functions and processing activities undertaken by CSPs must only be carried out within India, and the export of any type of data (including backups), is prohibited.
Separately, the Directions issued under the Information Technology Act, 2000 relating to information security practices, procedure, prevention, response and reporting of cyber incidents for Safe & Trusted Internet, among other cybersecurity and breach notification obligations, specifically require cloud service providers to register and maintain certain subscriber and customer related accurate
information for a period of 5 years after the cancellation or withdrawal of such subscriber's or customer's registration.
CONCLUSION
MeitY's empanelment process is detailed, fastidious, and imposes heightened obligations on cloud service providers that aim to contract with or otherwise offer solutions to players in the public sector. Accordingly, before seeking to tap into the public procurement processes, organisations that offer cloud services ought to undertake internal diligences to ensure that they are compliant with MeitY's requirements.
The content of this article is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter. Specialist advice should be sought about your specific circumstances.

New report urges defense agencies to adopt unified data observability
Technology leaders warn that legacy monitoring tools create critical blind spots across complex cloud architectures and are no longer sustainable to support autonomous and AI-dependent systems.
By Scoop News Group
September 22, 2026
Listen to this article
0:00
Learn more. This feature uses an automated voice, which may result in occasional errors in pronunciation, tone, or sentiment.
Scoop News Group graphic
Defense agencies expanding their use of artificial intelligence and autonomous systems face a mounting challenge: How to overcome the operational friction arising from the massive sprawl of distributed data systems. That sprawl contributes to critical blind spots and vulnerabilities across IT stacks. More fundamentally, it delays threat response times at a time when AI gives adversaries increased speed and capabilities.
To reduce those vulnerabilities and enhance mission readiness, military leaders need to execute a wholesale shift toward unified data observability, according to technical experts in a new report published by Scoop News Group and sponsored by Datadog.
Download the full report .
At issue is the need for real-time, unified observability of operational data across network infrastructure, applications, data storage and AI workloads to identify risks, investigate incidents autonomously and restore mission-critical services faster, says Chris Goings, strategic account executive for the Department of Defense at Datadog in the report. "As system complexity explodes, customers realize traditional monitoring is no longer sustainable. We need to be able to unify this data," said Goings.
To overcome these structural limitations, the report argues that defense agencies must replace isolated monitoring tools with a centralized telemetry architecture.
Traditional stand-alone monitoring tools that rely on deep table scans fail to process the dynamic telemetry generated by modern software-defined infrastructure and AI-enabled applications. In contrast, next-generation observability platforms continuously analyze metadata, logs, and telemetry across an agency's entire data ecosystem. Datadog's platform, for instance, can process trillions of data points per hour gathered from more than 1,000 native technology integrations into a unified view.
Clinging to fragmented legacy tools exposes defense operations to active operational risks, ranging from delayed threat response times to unbudgeted cloud expenditures. Unifying enterprise telemetry replaces inefficient "swivel chair management" - where operators lose critical time jumping between vendor-specific dashboards during security events - with a shared view of verified data across operations and cyber defense teams.
"Observability represents a fundamental evolution beyond traditional monitoring," said Joe Gavin, director of federal business at Datadog. "Where monitoring gave IT teams siloed views into the reliability and performance of their stack, observability unifies metrics, traces, and logs across every layer of the environment - enabling faster root cause analysis and significantly reducing mean time to resolution."
The report highlights several additional advantages of embracing unified data observability platforms for defense agencies, including:
Tracking ephemeral cloud workloads: Modern microservice architectures rely on cloud workloads that execute and vanish within seconds to optimize resource costs, leaving traditional monitoring tools with no path to trace past performance or security events, notes Rick Stewart, senior engineer at Datadog. "With Datadog, we can determine what happened at a specific time, what various workloads actually did during that ephemeral window, and why."
Accelerating Zero Trust and cyberthreat investigations: Historically, defense agencies lacked the capability to route operational and security log data efficiently to both operations and security teams through a single system. Modern observability platforms, such as Datadog's, can simultaneously alert operations and security teams about affected resources via filtered dashboards and provide recommendations to address issues, reducing the need for and the cost of multiple vendor monitoring tools.
Securing human-machine teaming and autonomous systems: As military forces field autonomous platforms and AI agents, the need for real-time visibility into system health, communication links, and model behavior becomes vital to mission assurance. Agent observability provides a zero-trust audit layer over autonomous activity. It can also track token consumption, detect model drift or anomalous outputs, and prevent unauthorized data access.
Additionally, by unifying telemetry data, agencies can consolidate operational, security and FinOps information onto a single, shared platform for greater data observability and cost control.
